title: Ambient-pressure superconducting conductors at room temperature

concept.text: The innovation would be a manufacturable superconducting material that works at ordinary atmospheric pressure and room temperature, formed into a bulk conductor such as a wire or tape. It would carry useful electrical current without measurable DC resistance while remaining superconducting under the magnetic fields, temperatures and mechanical conditions encountered in operation. The target is a usable conductor for cables, coils and electrical machines, rather than only a transition observed in a microscopic specimen.

Superconductivity requires both electron pairing and coherent collective behavior across the material. A high transition temperature alone does not establish a practical conductor: the material must also sustain sufficient current, tolerate the relevant magnetic field and remain chemically and structurally stable. For this concept, room-temperature operation means approximately 293 K or above; the earlier proposed minimum of 273 K would describe operation near the ice point and falls short of the title's goal. Reaching room temperature under sustained megabar pressure would demonstrate valuable physics but would not complete this ambient-pressure conductor innovation.

significance.text: A useful room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductor would remove refrigeration and sustained extreme pressure as operating requirements for the conductor. Its direct capabilities would include resistance-free DC conduction and persistent currents in suitable closed circuits. Making those capabilities available in a practical bulk material could transform the design of power equipment and magnets by removing a major materials constraint. This is a conditional judgment about its potential importance, not evidence that such a material has been achieved.

Compact high-field magnets, motors and generators would additionally require adequate critical fields, engineering current density, mechanical strength, reliable joints and protection against loss of superconductivity. Eliminating DC resistance in the conductor would not make a complete power link or machine lossless: operating losses and the performance of associated components would still matter. Superconductivity at room temperature would therefore be a powerful enabling property, rather than a guarantee of compactness, very high usable fields or inexpensive equipment.

Conditional downstream possibilities include redesigned electricity networks, magnetic transport, fusion magnets and other technologies that benefit from strong magnetic fields or superconducting circuits. Each would require its own engineering program, manufacturing capability and economic case. As an interpretive analogy, the advance would resemble a new bulk material that makes previously difficult engineering capabilities broadly accessible; the analogy does not establish that infrastructure would become cheap or that quantum machines would automatically improve.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is to combine strong pairing, sufficient phase coherence and a synthesizable, stable structure in a material that remains superconducting at room temperature after external pressure is removed. The March 2026 Perspective identifies no fundamental physical prohibition on room-temperature superconductivity. That theoretical permissibility does not establish that a suitable ambient-pressure material exists or provide a reliable recipe for making one.

Materials prediction must connect favorable electronic properties to a structure that can actually be synthesized and retained. A calculated structure's dynamical stability alone does not establish its thermodynamic accessibility, a workable synthesis route or persistence under ambient conditions. The supplied Perspective discusses predicted metastable, ambient-pressure high-temperature hydrides, including Mg2IrH6, that had not been experimentally demonstrated at its documented date. This is a gap for the predicted candidates discussed, rather than an exhaustive assertion about every hydride or every subsequent experiment.

An engineering breakthrough must accompany the materials discovery. The superconducting phase must survive fabrication into a continuous conductor and carry useful current across its full cross-section under an applied field. Chemical stability, thermal stability, mechanical integrity and repeatable preparation must persist beyond the conditions of an initial measurement. The pressure-quenched Hg-1223 results illustrate why retaining an enhanced transition at ambient pressure is a meaningful intermediate step while still leaving substantial barriers between a microscopic sample and a durable wire or tape.

current_state.text: The supplied papers identify the cuprate HgBa2Ca2Cu3O8+δ, commonly called Hg-1223, as reaching the longstanding ambient-pressure transition-temperature record of 133 K in 1993. A PNAS paper published on 9 March 2026 reports ambient-pressure resistive transition onsets of 139–151 K after pressure quenching Hg-1223. The samples were approximately 100–130 micrometers across. These are reported onset temperatures in microscopic specimens, not demonstrated operating temperatures for a manufactured conductor.

The pressure-quench study also describes a sample retrieved from the pressure cell, so confinement inside a diamond anvil cell should not be attributed to all the results discussed here. Magnetic measurements of the recovered sample showed a lower transition near 140 K, rather than magnetic confirmation at the maximum 151 K resistive onset. The enhanced phase had limited thermal stability. Even the highest reported onset remains far below both the ice point and room temperature.

For high-pressure hydrides, the supplied La-Sc-H manuscript reports reproducing a transition to zero resistance at 248 K in binary La-H at 170 GPa, consistent with the research summary's approximate value of 250 K. It also reports La-Sc-H onset temperatures of 271–298 K at 195–266 GPa. The arXiv record was first submitted on 29 September 2025 and revised on 6 October 2025; the supplied review concerns the revised manuscript, and does not establish that every reported result appeared in the initial submission. No journal version was identified in the supplied material.

These hydride measurements used diamond anvil cells and therefore do not establish ambient-pressure operation. The manuscript reports transport measurements and suppression of the transition by magnetic field, but lacks direct Meissner characterization. It also describes instability near its lowest pressures and an abnormal circuit response near 195 GPa. The 271–298 K range should consequently remain an attributed preprint report, with those experimental qualifications, rather than an independently certified demonstration across the entire range.

None of the supplied papers establishes superconductivity near 300 K at one atmosphere. This conclusion is limited to the supplied evidence: the record does not document a literature-wide freshness search through 1 November 2026, and it provides no evidence with which to assess the earlier assertion about LK-99 replication. Those evidence gaps neither establish the missing conductor nor show that a particular unassessed result is false.

The supplied review used complete main-article text for both PNAS papers, superseding the earlier research's publisher-access limitation. The pressure-quench paper's separately referenced supplementary appendix was not supplied, and figures and supplementary plots were not visually inspected. For the hydride preprint, all 41 manuscript pages were represented in the extraction, but PDF parser warnings led the review to treat access as partial. The quoted numerical passages were available despite those warnings. These are assessments of the authors' reported results from the supplied review, not independent remeasurement or a new inspection of the underlying documents.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration, not an established standard: at least two independent laboratories should reproducibly prepare a conductor measured in centimeters or more that operates at approximately one atmosphere and at or above 293 K. Each should demonstrate resistance consistent with zero within a stated measurement floor, together with either a Meissner effect or a persistent current lasting for hours. The preparation method, sample composition, geometry, measurement conditions and uncertainty should be documented well enough for another laboratory to reproduce the result.
completion_criteria.label: Two laboratories reproduce centimeter-scale superconductivity near one atmosphere, ≥293 K

completion_criteria.text: Proposed engineering demonstration: measure engineering current density for the complete conductor cross-section at a specified temperature and applied magnetic field, then use the conductor to generate a declared laboratory-scale magnetic field in a documented coil geometry. The field target and operating conditions should be specified before judging success; the supplied material does not justify inventing a universal numerical requirement. Repeat operation and thermal stability should be demonstrated, with clear boundaries for current, field, temperature, mechanical loading and duration.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate engineering current density and repeatable, thermally stable coil operation

completion_criteria.text: A resistivity drop alone, an isolated magnetic anomaly or a microscopic specimen requiring sustained diamond-cell pressure would not meet this proposed conductor milestone. A successful initial demonstration would still leave qualification for longer lengths, manufacturing consistency, joints, protection, service lifetime and cost. Finite experiments would establish performance across the tested operating range, rather than literal universality or readiness for every superconducting application.
completion_criteria.label: State tested operating limits and remaining conductor qualification requirements

related_concepts.text: Synthesis from the supplied roster: PHY-02, sustained net-electric power from controlled fusion, has a potential engineering connection through superconducting magnets. A room-temperature conductor with sufficient field tolerance, current capacity and mechanical performance could ease some magnet operating constraints. It would not establish fusion energy gain, reliable reactor operation or net electricity production, so the two innovations retain separate completion criteria.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: PHY-10, collider-quality plasma wakefield acceleration, concerns accelerating beams rather than discovering a superconducting conductor. Improved conductors could potentially benefit supporting magnetic equipment in an accelerator facility, but would not establish the beam quality or accelerator performance required by PHY-10. PHY-09, a coherent gamma-ray source, likewise concerns a distinct radiation-generation capability; the supplied evidence establishes no direct dependency between its achievement and PHY-01.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: PHY-03, a laboratory proof that gravity is non-classical; PHY-04, laboratory identification of the dark-matter particle; PHY-05, a tested microphysical account of the dark-energy scale; PHY-06, discovery of a magnetic monopole; PHY-07, observation of baryon-number violation; PHY-08, observation of lepton-number violation; PHY-11, a tested resolution of the black-hole information paradox; PHY-12, experimental identification of the physics that sets the Higgs-mass scale; and PHY-13, a tested mechanism for the cosmic matter excess, seek distinct discoveries about fundamental physics. Superconducting technology could be useful experimental infrastructure in some settings, but the supplied material establishes no specific dependency. Achieving PHY-01 would not supply the defining evidence for any of these entries.

Conceptual distinction from the supplied research and review: metallic hydrogen is a possible material identity, whereas PHY-01 is a functional conductor capability. A metallic-hydrogen material would overlap with PHY-01 only if it demonstrated the same ambient-pressure, room-temperature and useful-current requirements. The supplied evidence does not establish the earlier assertion about a claimed metastable metallic-hydrogen sample, and no separate roster entry is merged or removed on that basis.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish literature completeness or changes in the field through 1 November 2026.
Independent replication and long-term reproducibility of the pressure-quenched Hg-1223 enhancement are not established by the supplied material.

The supplied evidence does not resolve the full superconducting interpretation of the La-Sc-H onset range, particularly near the lowest reported pressures; direct Meissner characterization is absent from the reviewed manuscript.
The Hg-1223 supplementary appendix was not supplied, figures were not visually inspected, and the hydride PDF carried extraction warnings despite representation of all 41 pages.

The specific field, engineering current density, lifetime and manufacturing requirements for an application-ready conductor remain to be defined; the proposed initial demonstration is not a deployment qualification.
LK-99 replication and the earlier claimed metastable metallic-hydrogen sample cannot be assessed from the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Wires without resistance at room temperature
possible: Power cables could carry steady electrical current without resistance in the conductor, without refrigeration or extreme pressure. The material would work as a usable wire or tape at room temperature.
Magnets could maintain circulating currents without a continuing power supply in suitable closed circuits. Designers could build these capabilities into coils and electrical machines.
why: Removing cooling and pressure requirements would give engineers new ways to design power equipment and magnets. Electricity networks, magnetic transport and fusion research could benefit from conductors that work under everyday conditions.

sources.who: Rohit P. Prasankumar, Matthew Julian and collaborators
sources.showed: Their review identifies barriers to predicting materials that can actually be made and to controlling their superconductivity, the ability to carry steady current without resistance.
sources.cited_for: Finding a promising electronic structure is insufficient without a practical way to make and retain the material.
sources.not_established: The review provides no demonstrated material that combines room-temperature superconductivity with ordinary-pressure operation.

sources.who: Liangzi Deng, Ching-Wu Chu and collaborators
sources.showed: They reported the onset of superconductivity at 151 kelvin, far below freezing, in microscopic copper-based samples after rapidly releasing pressure.
sources.quote: a record-high ambient-pressure T c  up to 151 K achieved
sources.cited_for: An enhanced superconducting state can survive the removal of pressure.
sources.not_established: The highest onset lacked matching magnetic confirmation, and the enhanced state had limited thermal stability.

sources.showed: In a preprint, they reported room-temperature transition onsets in a lanthanum–scandium–hydrogen compound under extreme pressure, with zero resistance and a response to magnetic fields.
sources.quote:
Superconductivity, with a maximum onset temperature (Tconset) 
of 298 K, was confirmed by both the observation of zero electrical resistance and the suppression of Tc under 
applied magnetic fields.
sources.cited_for: Hydrogen-rich compounds offer a route toward superconductivity at room temperature.
sources.not_established: The work lacks direct evidence of magnetic-field expulsion, and instability complicates interpretation at the lowest pressures.

shown: Liangzi Deng and colleagues retained an enhanced superconducting state at ordinary pressure in microscopic samples. Their highest reported electrical transition onset remains far below room temperature.
Yinggang Song and colleagues reported transition onsets reaching room temperature under extreme pressure. Their preprint does not demonstrate operation after that pressure is removed.
missing: A material must remain superconducting at room temperature under ordinary atmospheric pressure.
The material must survive fabrication into continuous wires or tapes and carry useful current throughout the conductor in a magnetic field.
Repeatable manufacturing must preserve chemical stability, thermal stability and mechanical strength.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce room-temperature superconducting conductors
milestones.explanation: Two independent labs would have to reproduce centimeter-scale conductors at ordinary pressure and room temperature, with zero resistance plus magnetic-field expulsion or current persisting for hours. This would establish the basic capability.

milestones.label: A coil operates repeatedly with useful current and thermal stability
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to measure current across the whole conductor and demonstrate repeated, thermally stable coil operation against a declared magnetic-field target. This would establish performance under specified operating conditions.

milestones.label: Tests establish operating limits and remaining qualification needs
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish operating limits and identify remaining needs for longer conductors, consistent manufacturing, joints, protection, lifetime and cost. This would define what remains before practical use.

uncertain: It remains unknown whether a stable material with the required properties can be synthesized at ordinary pressure.
Independent laboratories have yet to establish reproducibility of the pressure-released copper-based material’s enhancement.
The current, magnetic field and lifetime needed to judge an application-ready conductor remain to be defined.

page.title: Ambient-pressure room-temperature superconducting conductors
page.definition: A continuous wire or tape carries direct current without measurable electrical resistance at 300 K and one atmosphere. Its superconducting material also exhibits the Meissner effect, the expulsion of magnetic flux on entering the superconducting state.

goal.need: Superconducting magnets serve about 40,000 MRI machines. CERN's LHC also requires the cryogenic infrastructure quantified below. Room-temperature superconducting conductors would remove refrigeration as a condition of zero-resistance transport. Replacing existing magnet conductors would additionally require matching their current and magnetic-field limits.

figures.caption: CERN's reported requirements for cooling the LHC superconducting magnets
figures.note: The electrical power is for the cryogenic system, not the superconducting conductor's resistive dissipation.

completion.title: A fabricated wire or tape carries superconducting current at 300 K and one atmosphere.
completion.criterion: A reproducibly fabricated continuous wire or tape carries nonzero DC transport current at 300 K and one atmosphere. Four-terminal measurements give voltage consistent with zero within stated uncertainty, and magnetic measurements establish Meissner flux expulsion in its superconducting material at the same temperature and pressure. An independent laboratory reproduces the preparation and superconducting transport in conductor form. This establishes a conductor demonstration; application-specific current, field, length and lifetime qualifications remain separate.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no combined acceptance test was found in the external documents searched.
completion.basis: Searched DOE's superconductivity workshop report, IEC 61788 wire guidance, and DOE/NREL CABLE Prize rules for a combined room-temperature, ambient-pressure wire acceptance test; none was found. DOE supplies the nominal 300 K temperature, and the Advanced Photon Source specifies one atmosphere. The fallback combines these conditions with superconductivity's electrical and magnetic signatures, without inventing minimum length, current density, field or lifetime.

milestones.title: A material superconducts above 77 K at ambient pressure.
milestones.criterion: A specimen exhibits zero-resistance transport and a superconducting magnetic response above the 77 K liquid-nitrogen benchmark at ambient pressure. Achieved: Wu and colleagues reported an 80–93 K transition in Y–Ba–Cu–O on 2 March 1987, using bars measuring 1 × 0.5 × 4 mm; the paper does not state the total number of bars tested.
milestones.set_by: American Physical Society, Physical Review Letters milestone collection, identifying superconductivity above liquid nitrogen's boiling point as a historical benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: a transition temperature higher than the 77 K boiling point of liquid nitrogen

milestones.title: At ambient pressure, a conductor material has a superconducting transition temperature of at least 160 K.
milestones.criterion: At ambient pressure, meet the temperature component of DOE's electric-power conductor materials target: superconducting transition temperature of at least 160 K, for intended operation at 120 K. This is a materials subtarget, not full conductor qualification. Deng and colleagues studied five HgBa2Ca2Cu3O8+δ specimens about 100–130 μm across and reported ambient-pressure resistive onsets of 139–151 K on 9 March 2026. A retrieved specimen had a magnetic transition near 140 K. Those results do not meet the 160 K target.
milestones.set_by: U.S. DOE Basic Energy Sciences workshop report, electric-power conductor materials target, temperature component only; ambient-pressure scope follows the Advanced Photon Source's applications requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote:
a transition temperature of at least
160 K is desirable.

milestones.title: A specimen shows zero resistance and Meissner flux expulsion at 300 K and one atmosphere.
milestones.criterion: At 300 K and one atmosphere, a specimen carries DC current with resistance consistent with zero and exhibits Meissner flux expulsion. Song and colleagues report 271–298 K onsets at 195–266 GPa in 13 runs, in the version dated 6 October 2025. Semenok and colleagues report seven unsuccessful alloy-based synthesis attempts at 250–280 GPa and no superconductivity at 245–300 K, on 20 August 2026. Both reports are preprints, not peer reviewed; different precursor preparation limits interpretation of the negative result. Neither establishes this ambient-pressure milestone.
milestones.set_by: Experimental superconductivity convention, summarized by IEEE Technology Navigator; DOE's workshop report supplies nominal room temperature of 300 K, and the Advanced Photon Source specifies ambient pressure as one atmosphere.
milestones.threshold_quote: conduct electrical current with exactly zero resistance and expel magnetic fields from their interior.

results.finding: Five Hg1223 specimens showed ambient-pressure resistive transition onsets of 139–151 K.
results.detail: A retrieved specimen also showed a magnetic transition near 140 K. The supplied text does not explicitly establish zero-resistance transport above 77 K; the resistance curves are in figures.
results.quote: Overall, T c s ranging from 139 K to 151 K were achieved at ambient pressure after PQP, in comparison with the original T c  ~133 K ( Right Inset ,  Fig. 1 B ) for Hg1223 before PQP.

results.finding: Five Hg1223 specimens showed ambient-pressure resistive transition onsets of 139–151 K.
results.detail: The reproducible onsets fall below 160 K. One specimen showed a possible 172 K transition, but it was not reproduced and its nature remains unresolved.
results.quote: Overall, T c s ranging from 139 K to 151 K were achieved at ambient pressure after PQP, in comparison with the original T c  ~133 K ( Right Inset ,  Fig. 1 B ) for Hg1223 before PQP.

results.finding: La-Sc-H hydride: 13 experimental runs reported superconducting onsets of 271–298 K.
results.detail: Measurements were made at 195–266 GPa, far above one atmosphere. The authors report zero resistance and magnetic-field suppression of the transition, but no direct measurement of Meissner flux expulsion.
results.quote:
Superconductivity with an onset temperature of 271-298 kelvin at 195-266 GPa is observed by 
the measurement of zero electrical resistance and the suppression of Tc under applied magnetic fields.

results.finding: Y–Ba–Cu–O bars, number unspecified, showed a superconducting transition between 80 and 93 K.
results.detail: Measurements were made at ambient pressure. The bars measured 1 × 0.5 × 4 mm; the paper does not state how many were tested.
results.quote:
A stable and reproducible superconductivity transition between 80 and 93 K has been unambiguously
observed both resistively and magnetically in a new Y-Ba-Cu-0 compound system at ambient pressure.

results.finding: One Sr-Ca-Li-intercalated graphite sample showed a possible superconducting transition near 350 K.
results.detail: The transition was observed at ambient pressure, but its superconducting origin remains unconfirmed. The authors report a high-temperature fraction below 0.1% and no substantial resistivity change at the transition in another sample.
results.quote:
For instance, Sample IIIc exhibits a high-Tc 
transition near 350 K (Fig. 2c).
